summary.text: An antibody, or immunoglobulin, is a large Y-shaped protein the immune system uses to identify and neutralize antigens such as those on bacteria and viruses.
Each antibody tip has a binding site that fits one particular part of an antigen, so it can tag the target for attack by immune cells or neutralize it directly.
Plasma cells secrete huge quantities of antibody, and in humans antibodies come in five classes: IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, and IgM.

facts.label: Five classes
facts.value: IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, and IgM

facts.label: Binding site
facts.value: A paratope, found on each tip of the Y

facts.label: Bound part of antigen
facts.value: A specific part called an epitope

facts.label: Plasma cell lifespan
facts.value: Long-lived ones can last an organism's whole life

items.prompt: A virus has a part it needs in order to invade host cells. How can an antibody stop it without help from other immune cells?

options.label: By binding to that part so the virus cannot use it
By digesting the virus with enzymes it carries
By turning the virus into a harmless B cell
By making the host cell shed its outer layer

items.explain: Antibodies can neutralize an antigen directly, for example by blocking a part of a virus essential for invading a host cell.

items.prompt: An antibody can latch onto one precise part of an antigen and ignore thousands of others. What gives it this precision?

options.label: The nearly unchanging base of its structure
Binding sites at the tips of its branches
The class it belongs to, such as IgG
Its ability to divide like a plasmablast

items.explain: Each branch of the Y has a paratope that binds one particular epitope, and the tips vary widely while the rest is much less variable.

items.prompt: Months after an infection, a person still has antibodies to that germ in their blood, though the germ is gone. What explains this?

options.label: Antibodies copy themselves once they are made
Short-lived plasmablasts persist for decades
Plasma cells keep secreting antibody without antigen
The antigen is stored in bone marrow as a reminder

items.explain: Plasma cells secrete huge quantities of antibody whether or not antigen is present, as long as they stay alive.

items.prompt: Mouse IgG1 acts more like human IgG2 than human IgG1. Why does this matter to researchers?

options.label: It complicates using animal models to study antibodies
It shows mice have no antibodies of their own
It proves all antibody classes work the same way
It means mouse antibodies cannot bind antigens

items.explain: Classes may share names between species while differing in function and distribution, which complicates animal models.

items.prompt: After an infection, what two paths can a B cell take as it differentiates?

options.label: Neutrophil or eosinophil, both phagocytes
Antigen or epitope, both binding targets
Paratope or isotype, both antibody parts
Antibody-secreting cell or memory B cell

items.explain: B cells can progressively differentiate into antibody-secreting cells or into memory B cells.

items.prompt: Why are antibodies generally counted as part of the adaptive immune system?

options.label: They are the first response seen in all animals
They are highly specific, rearranged, and reflect memory
They are encoded directly in the germline genes
They work only without the complement system

items.explain: They show exceptional specificity, are produced through genetic rearrangements rather than direct germline coding, and manifest immunological memory.

paragraphs.heading: A protein that finds targets
paragraphs.text: An antibody, also called an immunoglobulin (Ig), is a large protein that the immune system uses to find and neutralize antigens, such as those on bacteria and viruses. The word antigen blends "antibody generator", and antigens of almost any size or chemical makeup can be recognized. Each antibody recognizes one or more specific antigens.

paragraphs.heading: How it grabs its target
paragraphs.text: An antibody is shaped roughly like a Y. The tip of each arm carries a paratope, the binding site, which fits exactly one epitope, the particular part of an antigen it latches onto. Once bound, the antibody can tag the antigen, or a microbe or infected cell carrying it, for attack by immune cells. It can also neutralize the target directly, for example by blocking the part of a virus it needs to invade a host cell. So that the immune system can recognize millions of different antigens, paratopes come in an equally wide variety.

paragraphs.heading: The parts of the Y
paragraphs.text: Antibodies are heavy proteins of about 150 kDa and about 10 nm in size, made of three globular regions. In humans and most other mammals, one antibody unit has four polypeptide chains, joined by disulfide bonds: a matching pair of heavy chains and a matching pair of light chains. The two arms are the antigen-binding fragments (Fab), and the trunk of the Y is the crystallisable fragment (Fc). A flexible hinge between them lets antibodies grab pairs of epitopes at different distances and bind effector molecules more easily.

paragraphs.heading: Five classes
paragraphs.text: Apart from the tips, the rest of an antibody varies much less. Human antibodies fall into five classes, also called isotypes, named IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG and IgM, and IgG and IgA are split further into subclasses. The class decides which functions the antibody sets off, called effector functions, and also where in the body and at what stage of a response it is released. Classes with the same name can behave differently in other species: mouse IgG1 works more like human IgG2 than human IgG1.

paragraphs.heading: Where antibodies come from
paragraphs.text: Antibodies are made by antibody-secreting cells, a term covering plasmablasts and plasma cells. During an immune response, B cells can develop into these cells or into memory B cells. Plasmablasts multiply fast and live briefly, and they appear early in a response. Plasma cells do not divide, yet they release huge amounts of antibody whether or not antigen is around, and long-lived ones can potentially survive for the organism's whole life, classically in niches in the bone marrow.

paragraphs.heading: Part of adaptive immunity
paragraphs.text: Antibodies are generally counted as part of the adaptive immune system. They are highly specific, they are produced through genetic rearrangements rather than being written directly in the germline, and they reflect immunological memory. Memory B cells can last for decades and be called up quickly in a second response. The picture is not perfectly tidy, though: natural IgM, made by B-1 cells, recognizes many unrelated antigens and works with the complement system early in a response, acting more like innate immunity.
